summary: Source-anchored research for Counter-document pattern. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Replace a repeatedly requested computed value (such as a count or total) with a value stored in the database ahead of time and updated on writes that change the source data (or periodically), so a request needs only one read. This is particularly appropriate when reads are significantly more common than writes. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-patterns/computed-values/computed-schema-pattern/

$inc is atomic within a single document, but atomicity does not guarantee unlimited throughput on one global counter. MongoDB storage documentation describes that writers staging uncommitted writes to the same document concurrently may conflict and be retried under optimistic concurrency control, and a MongoDB Community Forums reply cautions that a single counter document could be a bottleneck. Treat the hot-document risk as workload-dependent, without deriving a universal throughput ceiling. (high confidence) Sources: https://github.com/mongodb/mongo/blob/master/src/mongo/db/storage/README.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/update/inc.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/how-to-implement-an-auto-incremental-id-in-an-environment-of-100-isertions-per-minute/215720

One practitioner proposal spreads increments across documents keyed by thread and time window, then aggregates older windows into a central total. This is an unbenchmarked contention-reduction design lead, not a verified exactly-once algorithm: the proposed update-then-delete steps need their own failure handling before production use. (low confidence)

Use server-side $inc for concurrent increments to an existing counter document. Unlike clients reading a number and writing a replacement with $set, concurrent increments do not overwrite one another; the atomicity guarantee covers the single counter document. (high confidence)

Periodic recomputation of stored totals permits stale results between refreshes. An approximation policy can additionally reduce update frequency when exact values are unnecessary; choose and document the tolerated accuracy instead of presenting such a counter as an exact current count. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-patterns/computed-values/computed-schema-pattern/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-patterns/computed-values/approximation-schema-pattern/

Batching increments in local memory reduces database writes but leaves unsynchronized events vulnerable to process restart. This is an explicit approximation tradeoff and is unsuitable when exact real-time counts are required. (high confidence)

The mongoose-sequence README documents a separate counters collection, global and scoped sequences, and atomic sequence allocation. It also warns that insertMany bypasses the hooks needed to increment its counter. Sequence allocation is not a maintained live-document count, so this library is implementation evidence rather than a general count-query replacement. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

A stored counter or total does not stay current by itself: when a new source document is inserted, the computed value no longer reflects the data, so the application must either recompute it with every write that changes the source data or refresh it in a periodic job. Keeping the counter accurate for the exact population being queried (including deletes and documents moving in or out of that population) is an application-design inference, not something the documentation states. (medium confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-patterns/computed-values/computed-schema-pattern/

A separate source-document insert or delete and its counter adjustment are not automatically atomic together. For an all-or-nothing change across those documents, MongoDB supports multi-document transactions, which generally cost more than single-document writes. This is a design implication of maintaining computed data separately. (high confidence)
